note: Source subject is the chiefs (Thrasybulus only the most resolute); candidate makes Thrasybulus alone win over the soldiers and sail to Tissaphernes.
replacement: Meanwhile the chiefs at Samos, and especially Thrasybulus, had remained firmly resolved to recall Alcibiades from the moment he changed the government. At last, in an assembly, they won over the mass of the soldiers. The soldiers voted for the recall and amnesty of Alcibiades, and the chiefs sailed over to Tissaphernes and brought Alcibiades to Samos. They were convinced that their only chance of safety lay in Alcibiades drawing Tissaphernes away from the Peloponnesians and over to themselves. An assembly was then held. In it Alcibiades complained of his private misfortune in having been banished and lamented it. He spoke at great length on public affairs, raised their hopes for the future very high, and extravagantly magnified his own influence with Tissaphernes. His aims were to frighten the oligarchical government at Athens, to hasten the dissolution of the clubs, to increase his credit with the army at Samos and strengthen their own confidence, and finally to turn the enemy as strongly as possible against Tissaphernes and destroy the hopes they had placed in him. So Alcibiades held out to the army promises as extravagant as these: Tissaphernes had solemnly assured him that if he could only trust the Athenians, they would never go short of supplies while he had anything left, no, not even if he had to coin his own silver couch; and he would bring the Phoenician fleet, now at Aspendus, to the Athenians instead of to the Peloponnesians. But he could trust the Athenians only if Alcibiades were recalled to be his security for them.
